sections.normalized_html: Find, in radians, the argument of [MATH: z=-1+\textrm{i}\sqrt{3}.]
sections.readable_text: Find, in radians, the argument of [MATH: z=-1+\textrm{i}\sqrt{3}.]

sections.normalized_html:
Let's plot [MATH: z] in the complex plane.

The complex number [MATH: z] lies in the second quadrant of the complex plane. Therefore [MATH: \dfrac{\pi}{2}< \arg(z)< \pi.] If [MATH: \alpha] is the angle that [MATH: z] makes with the negative real axis, then [MATH: \tan α|= (sqrt(3))/(1); α|= \arctan (sqrt(3)); = (π)/(3)]

Therefore, [MATH: \theta=\arg(z) = \pi - \dfrac\pi 3 = \dfrac{2\pi}{3}.]

Item 11 — Example: Finding the Argument of a Complex Number in the Fourth Quadrant

Example Prompt:
Find, in radians, the argument of [MATH: z=1-\textrm{i}.]

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
Let's plot [MATH: z] in the complex plane.

[IMG: /graphics/7a01ec786ab6babe94411394c93496d3]

The complex number [MATH: z] lies in the fourth quadrant of the complex plane. Therefore [MATH: \dfrac{3\pi}{2}< \arg(z)< 2\pi.]

If [MATH: \alpha] is the angle that [MATH: z] makes with the positive real axis, then
[MATH: \alpha = \arctan\left(1\right) = \dfrac\pi 4.]

Therefore,
[MATH: \theta=\arg(z) = 2\pi - \dfrac\pi 4 =\dfrac{7\pi}{4}.]
